pages.text:
*From the Walk-Book of Highstep, Day 1, evening. Weather: fair, then loud. Distance: three miles. Direction: left. The Mayor has asked me not to write "left."*

By noon, the sun was high and the road was still going left. The village did not know what to do with a mountain that had made a choice, so they stood on the Green and made a committee. Mayor Marsh climbed onto a crate of aged cheddar, which was the highest thing available that did not involve climbing the rope tower, where Mo’s father was currently whistling and refusing to look down.

"Item one," said the Mayor, tapping her clipboard with a finger that did not quite fit in the space between the pages. "The mountain is off the Road."

"It is not off the Road," said a voice from the back. It was Mrs. Pell, holding a basket of eggs that wobbled dangerously. "It is merely... lateral."

"It is left," said the Mayor. "Item two: Panic. Item three: Solution. We are currently at Item One."

Tor took another step. The whole village swayed. Admiral the goat, who was chewing on the corner of the Mayor’s sash, let out a low, dignified baa, as if to say that this was all very improper, and then continued eating.
pages.image: A round woman in a tall hat and green sash stands on a wooden cheese crate in a village green, pointing a clipboard at a massive mossy mountain leg in the distance, while a large brown and white goat with a crooked horn chews on her green sash.

pages.text:
"Mountains do not have opinions," said the baker, wiping flour from his hands onto his apron. "It is a tremor. A ground-shake. The earth is settling."

"The earth does not settle in circles," said Mo’s father, still up in the tower. "It settles down."

Gran stepped forward. She did not shout. Gran never shouted. She simply opened the Walk-Book, a heavy thing bound in leather that smelled of ink and old paper, and cleared her throat. The crowd went quiet, because when the Stepkeeper cleared her throat, you listened.

"Eleven hundred and four Long Walks," she read, her blue-stained thumb holding the page flat. "Every single day, the direction is the same. Right, down, left, up. The Winter Hollows hold the hay. The Spring Meadows hold the seeds. If we go left, we go into the wild. There is no hay there. There are no seeds. There is only... wind."

Mo looked at the birch gap, still visible to the right, pale and empty. Tor was not looking at it. Tor was looking at something else.
pages.image: A tiny old woman with a long white braid and huge round spectacles holds up a large open book to a crowd of villagers, her expression serious, while a large brown and white goat looks on with one ear perked, ignoring the commotion.

pages.text:
"Mo," Gran said. "What do you feel?"

The crowd turned. Mo stood at the back, barefoot, his dusty toes gripping the grass. He pressed one heel into the earth, a habit he did when he was thinking hard.

"She is not lost," Mo said.

The silence was sudden and very loud.

"Mo," said the Mayor, her voice soft and careful, the way one speaks to a kitten that has found a candle. "I am sure you feel things. That is a gift. But a mountain is a mountain. It does not decide. It goes where the road goes. The road goes right."

"The road is a line," Mo said. "She is a living thing. She can decide."

Someone laughed. It was a gentle laugh, the kind you make when a child says the sky is blue and you know it is, but it is also green sometimes. Mo did not like it. It was worse than anger. Anger you could argue with. Laughter just rolled over you and kept going.
pages.image: A small wiry boy with warm brown skin and untidy black hair stands barefoot in a green poncho, looking up defiantly at a crowd of adults in a village, his expression stubborn and serious, while a large goat stands close to his side.

pages.text:
Junie stepped forward into the space between the people, her yellow scarf tied tight against the breeze. She looked at Mo, then swept her gaze across the crowd before settling back on him again.

"If she goes left," Junie said, her voice sharp, "and she does not come back, then we can leave."

The crowd murmured.

"We can stay," Junie added, before anyone could stop her. "We can build a house on the ground. One that stays still."

Mo stared at her. Junie looked down at her boots, her tool-belt clinking softly as she shifted her weight from one foot to the other.

"You cannot just leave Highstep," Mo said.

"Nobody said we would," Junie replied, though her eyes were fixed on something far away. "I said it could be a possibility."

It was not a possibility. It was a dream. And dreams, Mo knew, were dangerous things to have when you were standing on a moving mountain.
pages.image: A tall girl with dark brown skin and a big puff of black curls tied with a yellow scarf stands with her hands on her hips, looking away from a small boy in a green poncho, while a crowd of villagers in the background looks on with confused expressions.

pages.text:
That night, the moon hung high and the pines stood perfectly still, while Mo lay awake on the flat stone of the Footpost, pressing one bare heel hard into the rock to listen.

Tor walked. Step, step, step.

It was a slow, patient rhythm, nothing like the hurried, anxious shuffle of a creature in pain or the confused stumbling of a lost thing. It was a walk with purpose. It was a walk with a destination.

*I know where I am going,* the steps said, speaking plainly in the language of his soles.

Admiral the goat, who had followed Mo to the stone, was chewing on the hem of his poncho, and Mo did not stop him.

"Where?" Mo whispered.

Tor paused. The silence stretched, thick and warm, until slowly, she took two long steps.

It was the first answer she had ever given him.
pages.image: A small boy lies on a flat stone in the moonlight, one bare foot pressed firmly to the ground, his eyes closed in concentration, while a large brown and white goat chews on the edge of his green poncho, the moon casting long shadows among the pines.
